title: We asked too much of the American university
gist: Noah Smith argues that as America's unifying institutions — churches, a mass military, lifetime-employment corporations, mass media, public transit — decayed between 1970 and 2020, mass higher education was drafted into replacing all of them, a role universities were never designed for. The binding constraint is that not everyone can complete college, which forced grade inflation as the release valve (Denning et al. find it explains most of the rise in graduation rates) while enrollment by recent high school graduates has fallen back to early-1990s levels. The text cuts off at a paywall partway through the argument.

insights.claim: The institutions that once bound Americans together across social classes — churches providing networking, matchmaking, day care and mutual aid; a mass wartime military; corporations offering lifetime employment; mass media; and public transit — all weakened substantially in the half-century from 1970 to 2020.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Institutional decay is the structural backdrop to American political fragmentation, which is the source of the policy volatility investors now have to price.
insights.locator: The United States used to have a bunch of institutions

insights.claim: Church attendance declined slowly and then fell off a cliff in the 2010s, while the military shrank into a small professionalized volunteer force and corporations ended their brief flirtation with lifetime employment and outsourced many of their roles.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The 2010s inflection in religious participation lines up with the era's social and political disruption — a dating marker for when the cohesion trend broke.
insights.locator: In the half-century from around 1970 to 2020

insights.claim: The share of Americans aged 25 to 29 holding a bachelor's degree rose from 16.4% in 1970 to 39.6% in 2020, and around two out of three have completed some college — mass attendance, not universities themselves, is the new phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A 23-point jump in degree attainment in fifty years is the demand curve behind the entire higher-education revenue and student-debt complex.
insights.locator: From 1970 to 2020, the share of Americans age 25-29

insights.claim: Mass enrollment inadvertently but inevitably thrust the role of broad socially unifying institution onto American universities — college became the new church, the new military, and the neighborhood bowling alley all rolled into one, with administrators rather than preachers homogenizing values.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If universities are load-bearing for social cohesion rather than merely for credentialing, political attacks on them carry second-order costs far beyond enrollment numbers.
insights.quote: College became the new church, the new military, and the neighborhood bowling alley all rolled into one.
insights.locator: This expansion inadvertently but inevitably thrust a new role

insights.claim: Americans increasingly delayed sex until college and many of those relationships turned into marriages, making the university the primary venue for household formation as well as education.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Ties falling college enrollment to downstream family formation and, ultimately, fertility — a demographic transmission channel that is rarely modeled.
insights.locator: Instead of meeting their first love in high school

insights.claim: American universities layered the German research model — a lab apprenticeship system producing cutting-edge basic research — onto an inherited British teaching model designed to educate and mentor the upper class.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The dual mandate explains why US universities are simultaneously consumer businesses and national research infrastructure — and why pressure on one side transmits to the other.
insights.locator: Our universities began as essentially a copy of the British model

insights.claim: The hybrid model enabled a remarkable cross-subsidy: undergrad tuition, state support and alumni gifts funded grad stipends, lab facilities and professor salaries, while prestige from famous researchers let universities charge undergrads more.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US basic research is financed by undergraduate demand, so any sustained enrollment or tuition decline is a direct hit to national research capacity.
insights.locator: This dual system enabled a remarkable form of cross-subsidization.

insights.claim: Universities used their prestige to attract high-paying, highly skilled foreign students from around the globe, which is part of how they kept thriving while America's other institutions came under pressure.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: International student flows are a named pillar of the funding model, making visa and immigration policy a direct financial risk to university balance sheets and research output.
insights.locator: especially once they used their prestige to attract high-paying

insights.claim: American universities held a lock on both the nation's research output and its production of human capital, and those two roles were mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Monopoly positions in both research and talent formation mean there is no ready substitute if the model breaks — the reason degradation here is a macro-relevant risk.
insights.locator: Universities became the lynchpin of America’s research effort

insights.claim: Confidence from successfully handling education and research simultaneously probably led universities to overreach into social and cultural roles, spending more and more on dorms and student services and hiring administrators at an astonishing rate.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Administrative and amenity cost growth is framed as a consequence of mission creep, not mismanagement — meaning cost discipline requires shedding roles, not just cutting budgets.
insights.locator: Colleges spent more and more on dorms and “student services”

insights.claim: The basic problem with college as America's primary unifying institution is that not everyone can go: completing coursework requires raw intelligence plus work ethic and independence, traits not everyone has and that we do not yet know how to instill.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A hard capability ceiling on enrollment means degree-attainment targets cannot be met without standard-loosening — which caps the credential's signalling value and its wage premium.
insights.quote: There was just one basic problem with college as America’s primary unifying institution, which is that not everyone can go to college.

insights.claim: Universities have necessarily become less and less selective as they absorbed a larger fraction of young Americans, and there is a limit to how far enrollment and completion can expand without loosening standards.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Declining selectivity across the sector devalues the median degree while concentrating value in a small elite tier — a widening bifurcation in higher-ed pricing power.
insights.locator: Universities have necessarily become less and less selective

themes.theme: Grade inflation as the release valve

insights.claim: Denning et al. (2021) find that most of the increase in US college graduation rates can be explained by grade inflation rather than changing student characteristics or institutional resources, and that at a public liberal arts college grades rose even holding performance on identical exams fixed.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising graduation rates are not evidence of rising human capital, which undermines the standard justification for expanding subsidized enrollment.
insights.quote: We find that most of the increase in graduation rates can be explained by grade inflation, and that other factors such as changing student characteristics and institutional resources play little or no role.

insights.claim: Colleges responded to the completion problem by implementing grade inflation from the 1990s onward, making it easier to finish a degree without learning the material well — but that process eventually hits a wall because a large fraction of young Americans is not prepared for college even with inflated grades.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The adjustment mechanism that sustained enrollment growth is exhausted, which is why enrollment has stopped rising regardless of policy support.
insights.locator: In fact, loosening standards is exactly what American colleges have done.

insights.claim: College enrollment by recent US high school graduates plateaued in the early 2000s and actually fell back to early-1990s levels during and after the pandemic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A thirty-year round trip in enrollment rates is a direct revenue headwind for tuition-dependent institutions and for the cross-subsidy that funds research.
insights.locator: College enrollment by recent high school graduates plateaued

insights.claim: The American university is described as the country's one remaining functional institution and it is now going downhill, with the model that made it the lynchpin of both research and social cohesion under threat.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames higher-education distress as a systemic rather than sectoral problem — watch small-college credit, research funding flows and international enrollment as the transmission points.
insights.quote: Our one remaining functional institution is going downhill.
